articles.title: Twenty-Five years later, Hollywood is giving 9/11 the silent treatment, and it’s making us less safe
articles.summary: The absence of September 11 films left a vacuum filled by conspiracy theorists, while filmmakers rallied for Gaza instead of grappling with terrorism.
articles.body: I am a historian, but you don’t need a PhD to realize that Americans and Brits learn most of what we know about the world from the movies. When most people think about World War II, for example, we think about the first few minutes of Stephen Spielberg’s Saving Private Ryan, or this summer, we are discovering the critical role of the chief Allied meteorologist, Captain James Stagg, through the new film, Pressure. We learned all about Vietnam from Apocalypse Now, Full Metal Jacket and Platoon. And Glory did more to make the Civil War feel accessible and immediate than even the best histories on that seminal conflict. Which is why it’s not only dispiriting but, frankly, deeply concerning that even now, a quarter of a century later, we’ve had so few movies about the attacks of September 11, 2001. 9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS True, Oliver Stone gave us World Trade Center, and Paul Greengrass United 93, both celebrations of ordinary Americans making extraordinary sacrifices on that fateful day. But other than these two dramas and a handful of notable documentaries, the great cultural machine that, for nearly a century, had told us the stories we needed to hear to make sense of ourselves and the world went largely silent. In fact, the last feature film on 9/11 was made over a decade ago, with none currently in the pipeline. Why? It’s a fascinating question, one that’s likely to keep future historians busy. You can blame it on progressive sensibilities, a DEI mindset, and not wanting to risk being accused of Islamophobia by producing movies that make Muslims look like the bad guys. DEAN CAIN SAYS HOLLYWOOD'S WOKE ERA IS ENDING: 'WE'LL LOOK BACK AND SAY THAT WAS STUPID' You can blame it on post-modernism, which favors irony and metaphor over direct engagement with difficult topics. When asked why he’d never made a movie about 9/11, for example, Spielberg replied that he had: 2005’s War of the Worlds, which features many scenes of urban devastation, but which does very little to help us think seriously about one of the most challenging moments in American history. You can blame it on the way movies are financed these days, with money coming in from investors all over the world, including from countries that aren’t really interested in heralding the values of the West. But whatever the reason, the bottom line remains the same: By failing to make movies that grapple with the reasons for and the responses to 9/11, Hollywood has made America and its allies weaker, more vulnerable and less safe. How so? Let us count the ways. US ARMY HITS 2026 RECRUITING GOALS FOUR MONTHS EARLY, PETE HEGSETH ANNOUNCES AT WEST POINT COMMENCEMENT First, look at the rates of enlistment to the U.S. armed forces. In 1986, for example, Navy recruiters saw a whopping 500% spike in young people eager to enlist — they had all watched Top Gun and left the theater thinking that naval service was not just worthy but desirable. Enlistment numbers remained solid throughout the 1990s and immediately after 9/11, but the early 2000s showed a drastic decline with the recruiting crisis reaching its peak in 2022-23. Hollywood’s failures, however, run even deeper. No serious person, patriotic as they may be, could argue that Hollywood has any obligation to reflect this ideology or that. But most serious people should argue that filmmakers are artists, and as such are at their finest when they grapple with the most pressing eras of their time. We consider Casablancaa classic, for example, in large part because it was filmed and released in the middle of World War II, giving us unforgettable characters that resonated with us precisely because they were forced to ask themselves who we were fighting and why. And when artists stop asking these questions seriously, moral confusion ensues. AS AMERICAN PRIDE HITS A 25-YEAR LOW, A NEW 9/11 EDUCATION PLATFORM URGES THE NATION TO NEVER FORGET We knew the Nazis were bad because we had decades of movies exploring their wickedness. And even if we couldn’t agree on the scope of American military engagement in Southeast Asia, no serious Hollywood filmmaker thought it wise to glorify the Vietcong or their supporters. The result was a culture that could have robust disagreements about important questions without losing track of the fact that America was a benevolent nation doing its best to safeguard freedom, democracy, and the other virtues of Western civilization. When Hollywood went silent and stopped making thoughtful movies about our wars, it created a huge cultural vacuum. And because nature abhors a vacuum — life, as a famous Hollywood movie once put it, always finds a way — that vacuum was filled by conspiracy theories. Crackpots like Alex Jones and Candace Owens and Tucker Carlson can only thrive because people need stories to help them make sense of the world, and if serious filmmakers won’t tell them, then the lunatics sure will. If that wasn’t bad enough, the same filmmakers who had so shamefully failed to wrestle with our recent history added insult to injury by showing up en masse, in the aftermath of Oct. 7, 2023, to advocate not for America and its challenges but for Gaza, currently governed by a terror group that shares an ideology with the Jihadis who attacked us 25 years ago this month. This is all very depressing. But if you’ve watched even a handful of good, old-fashioned Hollywood movies, you know that a setback in act II almost always becomes an opportunity in act III. The same technology that gave us AI slop can also be used to tell more ambitious stories more cheaply. And if Hollywood had taught us anything, it’s that heroes are never in short supply in America.

articles.title: Prince Harry finds way to live ‘half-in, half-out’ life Queen Elizabeth refused to endorse: experts
articles.summary: Prince Harry and Meghan's U.K. return with their children echoes the "half-in, half-out" proposal Queen Elizabeth II rejected at Sandringham.
articles.body: Prince Harry may have finally found a way to live the life that his grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, refused to endorse. On Sept. 8, 2022, Britain's longest-reigning monarch died after 70 years on the throne. She was 96. On Aug. 26 this year, Harry and his wife, Meghan Markle, returned to the U.K., where their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, will attend school. As the Sussexes settle into their new life in Britain, with details about their private home and their children's school closely guarded, royal experts told Fox News Digital that the arrangement recalls the "half-in, half-out" proposal the late queen rejected. PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK MOVE PUTS FRESH SPOTLIGHT ON THEIR EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS AGAINST ROYAL FAMILY "Harry may feel vindicated because, superficially, he has created something resembling the freedom he originally wanted," Kinsey Schofield, host of the YouTube show "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. "But I think calling it a victory misunderstands what the queen rejected." "I see absolutely no reason to believe she would have changed her mind," Schofield said. "Queen Elizabeth spent 70 years protecting the distinction between the crown and the individual. It seems unlikely that one of the defining judgements of her final years would suddenly have become negotiable." While the Sussexes have returned to the U.K. for an extended stay, they won't resume their roles as working royals. They will live in a private, non-royal residence outside London while maintaining their California home and a property in Portugal. People magazine reported that Meghan is in early talks for a role in the Netflix drama "The Gentlemen." WATCH: PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE CAUSED QUEEN STRESS IN FINAL YEARS: AUTHOR On Monday, the Lord Chamberlain, the most senior official in the royal household, sent a letter to senior officials in the government and military, as well as lord lieutenants, the king's personal representatives around the country. The letter drew a firm line around the Sussexes’ homecoming, reaffirming that the couple will not resume official duties. "It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of The Sovereign, and are no longer working Members of The Royal Family," a letter sent on behalf of King Charles III read, Fox News can confirm. "This position, distinct from the State and Royal duties undertaken by the working Royal Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected." "It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex," the letter added. "Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and are not used. The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity. In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests." The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals in 2020 after describing intense scrutiny from the British press and saying they lacked support from the palace. "Following conversations with the duke, the queen has written confirming that in stepping away from the work of the royal family it is not possible to continue with the responsibilities and duties that come with a life of public service," a statement from Buckingham Palace read at the time. In response, the couple issued a statement of their own, saying: "We can all live a life of service. Service is universal." British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital the queen drew a firm line before the couple's departure, insisting the Sussexes could not be "half in, half out" as working royals. "Her position was simply stated as ‘all in or all out,’" Fordwich said. "While King Charles has maintained that position, he is likely to be more open to private reconciliation and family gatherings, especially if Harry refrains from further public attacks on the family. Prince William, however, remains resistant to any formal restoration of royal duties for Harry." In 2020, Harry attended the Sandringham Summit at Queen Elizabeth II's Norfolk estate, where senior royals determined the terms of his and Meghan's departure from royal life. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE According to People magazine, it was there that the late queen made her position clear. After lengthy discussions, Harry was told there would be no "half-in, half-out" role for the Sussexes. They could not remain working royals while also pursuing independent, income-generating ventures. In his memoir "Spare," Harry recalled the Sandringham meeting and wrote that he believed the royals would consider five options for the Sussexes. "Option Five" called for a full departure. After about an hour, the queen's private secretary — nicknamed "The Bee" by Harry — distributed drafts of a statement announcing "Option Five." Harry wrote that he was stunned. "Wait. I'm confused," he wrote. "You've already drafted a statement? Before any discussion? Announcing Option Five? In other words, the fix was in this whole time? This summit was just for show?" Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital he believes the palace made a mistake by rejecting the proposal outright. "In my view, the queen was very badly advised by her representatives over the ‘half in, half out’ policy," he said. "I cannot see any reason in this day and age why it could not work. It shows a level of hypocrisy. Harry and Meghan could have remained in the royal fold without costs to the public purse. And yet, this was deemed unacceptable." Schofield argued the queen had good reason to reject the proposal. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "The queen had already learned the dangers of ‘half in, half out’ long before Harry and Meghan proposed it," she explained. "Prince Edward and Duchess Sophie attempted to maintain commercial careers alongside royal duties, with Edward running his television company and Sophie working in public relations. The arrangement became increasingly uncomfortable for the institution, especially as their professional lives generated headlines that risked trading on their royal connections. Ultimately, they abandoned those careers and became full-time working royals." "That experience demonstrated exactly why the lines need to be clear," Schofield continued. "You are either representing the Crown and accepting the restrictions that come with that privilege, or you are pursuing a private, commercial life. Trying to do both inevitably raises questions about royal status, access and whether relationships are being leveraged for personal gain." Schofield argued senior royals dedicate themselves fully to serving the crown and supporting the monarch as a united front. She said it would have been "unfair" to relax those restrictions for the Sussexes while allowing them to benefit from their royal status. In the queen's eyes, commercial freedom was "incompatible" with royal service. "The queen might have wanted more family connection with Harry and Meghan, but she wouldn’t have compromised the constitutional aspects of such an arrangement," Fordwich said. "She would also have been deeply wary of the commercial conflicts it could create. It would have set a precedent for other royals wanting to have it both ways." Before Harry and Meghan returned to Britain, Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," told Fox News Digital that a "hybrid" model was inevitable. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE "[The Sussexes] thought they could have a hybrid role of having a business life and a private life, while also spending a few months in the U.K. supporting the queen," he shared. "Harry believed that was an option, which was whipped away from him." WATCH: PRINCE HARRY BELIEVED ROYAL FAMILY COULD HAVE ALLOWED A ‘HYBRID’ ROLE: AUTHOR After stepping back from royal duties, the Sussexes signed lucrative deals with Netflix and Spotify and publicly aired their grievances in interviews, documentaries and Harry's memoir, further straining his relationship with the royal family. In 2025, Harry told the BBC he was ready for reconciliation and eager to spend more time with his father, who is being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer. According to a source close to the Sussexes, Meghan will continue leading her As Ever company from the U.K., while Harry will spend more time working with his U.K.-based charities. In July, the Sussexes privately met with the king at his Highgrove estate. It was the first time Archie and Lilibet had seen their grandfather since the late queen’s Platinum Jubilee in 2022. Schofield questioned whether Harry has any regrets about his grandmother's final years. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Harry says he loved his grandmother, and has spoken very warmly about their relationship," she said. "But some of his choices during her final years became part of an already difficult period for the royal family. Whatever grievances Harry had with the institution, his grandmother was elderly, recently widowed and approaching the end of an entire life of service. There are conversations he can never have with her and decisions he can never revisit with her." Fox News Digital's Lauryn Overhultz contributed to this report.

articles.title: Verstappen mistake made Monza 'awkward' for Piastri: 'It was tricky'
articles.summary: Oscar Piastri found the racing bizarre at the Italian Grand Prix after being involved in various yo-yo battles. Piastri crossed the finish line in fifth plac...
articles.body:
Oscar Piastri found the racing bizarre at the Italian Grand Prix after being involved in various yo-yo battles.

Piastri crossed the finish line in fifth place after being involved in various battles with Lewis Hamilton , Max Verstappen , and Lando Norris throughout the day.

Asked whether it was enjoyable from a driver's viewpoint, the Australian said: "It's difficult. Like, you know if you use any extra energy, you're gonna pay for it somewhere and I was kind of slowly building a gap on Lewis and then he spent all his energy getting past me and then kind of kept using it to try and break free and he actually got like a second ahead, and he lost it all in one straight.

"So it's still quite bizarre. Did I enjoy it more than I thought? Yes. Was I stuck in a lot of battles instead of having them pull me further into the race? Yes, I was also in that situation.

"So it is what it is. You know, probably better than a race where nothing happens, but definitely difficult in the cockpit to know exactly what to do."

Verstappen's mistake caused 'awkward' situation

Despite the Red Bull Racing driver being on fresher tyres, Piastri was able to keep up with Verstappen until he began battling Norris.

"He (Verstappen) made a bit of a mistake at Turn 1, and I think the track was breaking up quite a bit at Turn 2, and I think he got into marbles, and I think that took a while for him to get that off his side. So because of that, then we had a lot of back and forth and like, actually, I just wanted him to sit in front of me and drag me along because I knew he was quicker than me.

"But once that happened, it was a bit awkward because he was a little bit quicker but not enough to just, you know, for me to sit there comfortably and not have to compromise my driving. That was a bit tricky, but I think our pace at the end of the stint looked quite good, which was which was good."

articles.title: Volver a los orígenes: Williot presenta su colección otoño/invierno
articles.standfirst: La estética preppy, los códigos universitarios y su icónico logo regresan renovados en su nueva propuesta 2026
articles.summary: La estética preppy, los códigos universitarios y su icónico logo regresan renovados en su nueva propuesta 2026
articles.body: Hay prendas capaces de transportarnos a otro lugar: una sudadera con escudo, una chaqueta deportiva o un jersey de punto que evocan el imaginario universitario y han conseguido trascender generaciones. Porque mirar atrás no siempre es nostalgia; a veces, es simplemente reconocer de dónde venimos. Ese es precisamente el punto de partida de Williot para su nueva colección Otoño/Invierno 2026, que recupera algunos de los códigos que han construido la identidad de la firma para llevarlos al presente. Bajo el concepto 'No es nostalgia, es identidad', la marca vuelve a sus propias raíces y las reinterpreta desde una mirada actual, demostrando que aquello que forma parte de nuestro imaginario también puede seguir evolucionando. Si bien la industria del textil lleva años recuperando tendencias pasadas, Williot ha interiorizado ese espíritu en una colección donde el universo universitario es el hilo conductor de esta nueva propuesta. Ese estilo preppy que mezcla lo académico con una actitud más desenfadada encuentra en la firma una nueva lectura a través de tipografías tipo varsity, escudos bordados y bloques de color que remiten directamente a la estética universitaria norteamericana. Los reconocibles códigos del campus aparecen sobre sudaderas, chaquetas y prendas de punto, pero también conviven con siluetas más técnicas y actuales. Porque si algo demuestra esta colección es que lo clásico no tiene por qué quedarse anclado en otra época. Y, por supuesto, hay un elemento que permanece intacto: el doggy. El símbolo más reconocible de Williot vuelve a ocupar un lugar protagonista, reafirmando su condición de emblema de la firma y ese vínculo emocional que mantiene con quienes la llevan. Más que un simple detalle, su presencia funciona como una especie de hilo conductor entre las diferentes generaciones que han hecho suyo el universo de la marca. También los colores cuentan esta historia. El marino, el verde botella, el blanco roto y el burdeos recuperan una paleta profundamente ligada al legado de Williot y aportan ese aire heritage que conecta inmediatamente con el imaginario universitario. Son tonos que hablan de tradición, pero que aquí aparecen reinterpretados para formar parte de una propuesta pensada desde el presente. Esta colección no busca recrear el pasado, sino reinterpretar aquellos elementos que ya forman parte del ADN de Williot y darles una nueva vida, moviéndose entre la tradición y la modernidad, la disciplina universitaria y el desenfado contemporáneo. Porque hay estéticas que no regresan simplemente porque estén de moda, sino porque ya forman parte de nuestra cultura visual. Por eso, este Otoño/Invierno 2026, Williot recupera sus códigos más reconocibles para demostrar que mirar a las raíces también puede ser una forma de avanzar.

articles.title: Third Burning Man festivalgoer dies during final days of annual Nevada desert gathering
articles.summary: A third Burning Man festivalgoer died while being transported to a Reno-area hospital, following two earlier deaths at Black Rock City during this year's gathering.
articles.body: A third Burning Man festivalgoer has died after being transported to a hospital, authorities said, marking the latest death connected to the Nevada desert gathering after two men died at the festival within roughly 48 hours. Pershing County Sheriff Jerry Allen told Fox News Digital in an email that his office had received information about a third participant who died while being transported from the festival to a Reno-area hospital. Allen said he did not have additional information about the circumstances of the death, because it occurred outside his jurisdiction. He referred questions to the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office and Washoe County Medical Examiner’s Office. Fox News Digital has reached out to both for comment. TWO MEN DIE WITHIN 24 HOURS AT BURNING MAN AS TENS OF THOUSANDS GATHER IN THE NEVADA DESERT Authorities are also awaiting autopsy and toxicology results for the two men who died at Burning Man earlier in the festival. Allen said his office typically sees about one death each year at the festival. The first death was reported Thursday at Rampart, the temporary hospital at Burning Man, according to a Pershing County Sheriff’s Office news release. Festival organizers described the man as in his mid-50s. Deputies found Sampson Tshombe dead at the hospital after he was found on a street at the festival, the sheriff’s office said. Emergency personnel performed CPR for several minutes before a doctor pronounced him dead. Investigators found no external signs of foul play. Tshombe was taken to the Washoe County Medical Examiner’s Office for an autopsy and toxicology screening because authorities did not have his medical history. BURNING MAN MURDER MYSTERY DEEPENS AS NEW DETAILS EMERGE 1 YEAR AFTER DESERT FESTIVAL KILLING On Saturday, deputies were again called to Black Rock City, the temporary city built each year for Burning Man, after festival organizers said a 60-year-old man died. Craigh Mann was found dead in a trailer he shared with his significant other at about 3:17 p.m., according to the sheriff’s office. Investigators found no outward signs of foul play. Mann was also taken to the Washoe County Medical Examiner’s Office for an autopsy and toxicology screening. The sheriff’s office said investigators did not have his medical history or other information that could explain his death. The autopsy and toxicology results for both men are expected in six to eight weeks. The sheriff’s office said it would not release further information until it receives the results. Burning Man organizers previously said their "thoughts and deepest condolences" were with Mann’s family, friends, campmates and others affected by his death. "The safety and well-being of our community and staff remain our highest priority," organizers said after the first death, adding that support resources were available around the clock in Black Rock City. articles.title: La Oreja de Van Gogh anuncia que está trabajando en su nuevo disco de cara al próximo año: “No tenemos tiempo”
articles.standfirst: La banda donostiarra prevé sacarlo a la luz a lo largo de 2027
articles.summary: La banda donostiarra prevé sacarlo a la luz a lo largo de 2027
articles.body: Hace ya casi un año que Amaia Montero volvió para ponerse al frente de La Oreja de Van Gogh como vocalista tras la salida de Leire Martínez. Con el regreso de Montero, la banda donostiarra arrancó en 2026 la gira ‘Tantas cosas que contar’, con la que está recorriendo nuestro país y recuperando en directo los grandes éxitos de la primera etapa. Pues bien, una vez finalice esta gira, la propia banda musical, durante los Premios Juventud 2026 en Marbella del pasado jueves, 3 de septiembre, anunciaron que están trabajando en un nuevo disco. En el citado evento, Montero cantó ‘Rosas’, un single exitoso y también recibieron el reconocimiento de “Agente de Cambio” por su trayectoria en la gente española. Pues bien, sobre su nuevo trabajo se pronunciaron desde la propia banda, según unas declaraciones recogidas por Los 40. Después de un periodo exitoso de varios conciertos celebrados a lo largo por nuestro país, el grupo donostiarra ya mira a su gira por Latinoamérica a partir de 2027. Más allá de esto, están trabajando en su nuevo disco, del que se desconoce cuándo verá la luz, aunque todo apunta a que pueda ser el próximo año. La banda afronta esta nueva etapa convencida que las canciones siguen llegando al plano emocional de varias generaciones de seguidores, independiente de los años que pasen. Desde el propio grupo reconocen que “están en ello” y que tienen en mente “grabarlo” tras los conciertos y la gira mundial. La banda dice que lleva compuestas “varias canciones” y según apunta Amaia Montero: “El tema es llegar al estudio y grabarlas, pero no tenemos tiempo”. De esta manera, tan solo queda esperar para ver cuando se acaba haciendo este nuevo disco realidad, en declaraciones de la propia intérprete y la banda musical tras el evento en Marbella.

articles.title: Operan de urgencia al hijo de Melendi con solo 15 años
articles.standfirst: Sus padres no han desvelado qué es lo que ha ocurrido al adolescente
articles.summary: Sus padres no han desvelado qué es lo que ha ocurrido al adolescente
articles.body: El hijo de Melendi y Dámaris Abad, a quien se conoce de forma artística como Dama, de solo 15 años, ha sido operado de urgencia, como la propia cantante ha publicado en su perfil de Instagram. No han desvelado qué le ha ocurrido a Marco, como se llama el chico, aunque sí ha señalado que todavía les queda otro día en el centro hospitalario: “1o día superado. Vamos a por el 2º”, escribió en sus stories. “Operación de urgencias a mi niño, pero gracias a Dios todo está bien. Agradecida por la vida y teniendo presente que vivirla es un regalo precioso. Ánimo a todas las personas que están en un hospital”, prosiguió diciendo. Y es que la relación con sus padres es más que buena, sobre todo con Melendi, gracias a su pasión por la música, como el propio cantante de 47 años reconoció en uno de sus últimos conciertos en Albacete, invitándole a tocar la guitarra con él en el escenario para interpretar ‘Barbie de Extrarradio’. “Estoy muy orgulloso. Es muy difícil encontrar tu vocación, pero él desde pequeño lo tiene muy claro. Ya lee música, toca cuatro instrumentos, así que sabe hacia dónde va", señaló. Algo que su Dama también reconoce: “Está sabiendo elegir su camino y es muy maduro, tiene mucho talento", destacó en declaraciones a Europa Press. Además, su madre, en su 15 cumpleaños, le dedicó un post de Instagram: “Hijo mío 15 años… Cómo explicarte lo que siento al verte crecer, al verte convertirte en el mejor ser humano del mundo en todos los aspectos, cómo te explico tanta nostalgia de cuando eras un bebé y ahora tan mayor tan maduro e independiente, pero aún así siempre juntos, siempre tan cariñoso… Te amo tantoooo”. “Agradecida a Dios siempre por la maravillosa obra de la creación y el privilegio de poder ser MADRES que, para mí, no hay nada igual en esta vida que dar a luz y ver crecer a un hijo. Gracias eternas”, sentenció.
